opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot under the heading of gradual disempowerment. Right now, one of the main reasons we tolerate other people becoming very powerful or very rich is that there's a kind of positive-sum bargain built in. If someone builds a big company, they usually have to employ lots of people, they have to make products people actually want, and the growth of their power tends to spill over into more jobs, better wages, cheaper goods. So even if I'm a bit envious, I can see that their success is somewhat tied to mine. My labor is valuable to them, and that gives me leverage.

Now imagine a world where AI can do essentially all economically valuable work, and most people are living on some kind of universal basic income. That bargain sort of evaporates. The powerful no longer need my labor, and I'm no longer contributing to their success in any meaningful way. Meanwhile, my income is coming from a redistribution scheme that depends on political decisions, which in turn depend on whoever controls the AI systems and the resources.

So the question becomes: why would I tolerate someone accumulating more and more power if it doesn't benefit me, and if their accumulation actually threatens the very mechanism keeping me fed? In that world, someone else's growth in power starts to look much more zero-sum, or even negative-sum from my point of view. The rational response might be to be much more suspicious of concentrations of power, maybe to push much harder for constraints on it, because you no longer have the implicit guarantee that you'll stay relevant.

And the flip side is equally worrying. From the perspective of the people who hold power, the reasons to tolerate everyone else, to keep paying the UBI, to keep honoring democratic norms, also weaken. Historically, states treated citizens well partly because they needed them: as workers, as soldiers, as taxpayers. If AI replaces all of those functions, the incentive to keep humans empowered becomes more about goodwill or legacy institutions than hard necessity. And I don't think we should be very confident that goodwill alone holds up over decades of competitive pressure.

So I think UBI is a reasonable band-aid for the income problem, but it doesn't solve the leverage problem. It sort of makes you a pensioner of whatever system is running things, and pensioners don't have much bargaining power. That shifts the whole logic of why we put up with inequality and power concentration, and I don't think we've really reckoned with that yet.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing I want to point at is that, right now, most of us are in a position where we kind of have to tolerate other people getting more powerful, because we need them. Like, if some company is accumulating a huge amount of capital, or a billionaire is getting more and more influence, the reason that doesn't collapse into something terrible is partly that they still depend on everybody else. They need workers, they need customers, they need soldiers, they need taxpayers. And that mutual dependence is doing a lot of quiet work in keeping power somewhat distributed and somewhat accountable.

And I think the uncomfortable thing about a world with really advanced AI is that a lot of those dependencies start to go away. If the people at the top can get their labour from machines, their security from machines, even their companionship and status from machines, then the ordinary reasons they had to keep the rest of us on side get a lot weaker.

So then you say, OK, well, what about universal basic income? And I think UBI is often presented as the solution here — like, don't worry, the gains will be shared. And I do think it's probably necessary. But I'd want people to notice that it kind of flips the direction of dependence. Historically, the powerful depended on the many, and the many could withhold things. In a UBI world with AI doing the work, the many depend on the powerful, on whoever controls the systems and the transfers, and they have very little to withhold. You're not a participant in the economy that the elite needs, you're a recipient. And that's a very different bargaining position, even if your material life is quite good.

So to actually answer your question: I think the reasons for tolerating others getting more powerful shift from something like "I benefit from this and they can't get too far out of line because they need me" to "I'm relying on their continued goodwill, or on institutions constraining them, and I'm hoping those hold." And that second thing is much more fragile. It's basically a bet that the people or systems who end up in control stay nice, or stay constrained, indefinitely.

Which is why I think the question isn't really "should we have UBI or not" — it's more like, what else needs to be true for a world like that to stay stable? Do people still have some form of real leverage? Is there genuine competition and pluralism among the powerful actors, or does it consolidate? Are there mechanisms where, if things start going badly, ordinary people can actually do something about it, rather than just hoping the cheque keeps arriving? I don't think we have great answers to those yet, and I worry that UBI can feel like an answer in a way that makes people stop asking.

astra-6.text:
I think one reason we tolerate other people becoming very powerful is that we expect to benefit from what they do. Someone builds a company, and they get rich, but they also create jobs and make things that we want. So there’s at least a story about why this is good for everyone.

With advanced AI, that bargain could change. If you don’t need other people’s labour, then their bargaining power goes away. And a universal basic income might mean that everyone still gets enough to live on, but it doesn’t necessarily give them any say over what happens. You could be materially comfortable and still be entirely dependent on decisions made by a very small number of people.

So I think we’d want to ask: what are we getting in exchange for allowing that concentration of power? And can we arrange things so that people have an actual stake in the system, rather than just an income that somebody else has decided to provide?

sol-6.1.text:
I think one reason we tolerate other people becoming very powerful is that we expect to benefit from what they do. Someone builds a company, and it provides things we want, or employs us, or pays taxes. There’s at least some story about why their getting richer makes the rest of us better off.

With advanced AI, that connection could become much weaker. If you don’t need my labour, and I’m receiving a basic income, then we’re not really bargaining with each other in the same way. I might be materially comfortable, but I’m also dependent on a system that you have much more control over than I do.

So I think the question becomes: why would I want you to have even more power? If the answer is that it will grow the economy, but we already have plenty of goods, that’s less compelling. What I might care about instead is having a say in what happens, and knowing that my income and my freedom don’t depend on somebody else continuing to be generous. A basic income could address a lot of material needs without addressing that problem at all.
